Above means at a higher level or position than something else. Think of two things, one placed higher than the other — the one that is higher is "above" the other.

Everything else this word does is an extension of this simple idea of "being higher."

This is the most direct use. One thing is literally at a greater height than another.

  • The fan is above the table.
  • She held the torch above her head so everyone could see.
  • Dark clouds gathered above the city.
  • The painting hung above the fireplace.

Notice that "above" here means the two things don't have to be touching. The fan isn't resting on the table — it's hanging somewhere higher. This is important: above implies a gap in height, not contact.
2. More Than a Number or Amount

When talking about quantities — numbers, temperatures, ages, scores, levels — "above" means more than or exceeding a certain point.

  • Temperatures above 40°C can be dangerous.
  • Children above the age of 5 are allowed inside.
  • His score was above 90 in every subject.
  • Drive at a speed above 100 km/h and you'll get a fine.
  • Noise above 85 decibels can damage your hearing.

Think of it like a scale or a ruler. "Above 40°C" means the temperature is sitting higher on that scale than 40. The same logic from physical height now applies to numbers.
3. Higher in Rank, Power, or Authority

Just as one object can be physically higher than another, one person or position can be higher in a system of authority or rank. "Above" captures this.

  • A colonel is above a major in the army.
  • The CEO is above everyone else in the company.
  • In the old feudal system, lords were above peasants.

Here, "above" describes who has more power, a higher title, or greater authority.

This is where it gets more abstract but still follows the same logic. If something is high up and out of reach, it's untouchable. "Above" carries this idea — when something is above you, you can't grab it, affect it, or touch it.

The most famous example:

  • No one is above the law.

This means the law applies to everyone, no matter how powerful or important. Nobody is so high up that the law can't reach them.

More examples:

  • She thought she was above criticism. (She believed she was too important or perfect to be criticized — criticism couldn't "reach" her.)
  • The king acted as if he were above ordinary rules.
5. Too Good or Too Dignified to Do Something

This is closely connected to the previous meaning. When someone is "above" doing a certain thing, it means their character, morals, or dignity is at such a high level that they wouldn't lower themselves to do it.

  • He is above cheating. (His character is too good; he would never cheat.)
  • She is above petty gossip. (She is too mature or dignified to engage in it.)
  • A person of true integrity is above taking bribes.

Now pay close attention to "not above" — this flips the meaning completely. "Not above" doing something means the person is actually willing to do it, even if it's something slightly questionable.

  • He is not above bending the rules when it helps him. (He's perfectly willing to bend rules — he's not too dignified for that.)
  • She is not above telling a small lie to avoid trouble.

So:

  • "above doing X" → too good/moral to do X
  • "not above doing X" → willing to do X, even if it's not entirely honorable
6. More Important Than — Valuing One Thing Over Another

"Above" can show that one thing is considered more important, more valuable, or more worthy than something else.

  • He values honesty above everything else. (Honesty is the most important thing to him.)
  • She puts her family above her career.
  • For this job, skill matters above experience.
  • He prizes loyalty above all other qualities in a friend.

When a sound or voice is "above" the noise around it, it means it is loud enough to be heard clearly despite the surrounding noise — as if it rises higher than the other sounds.

  • She had to shout above the noise of the crowd.
  • I could hear his voice above the music.
  • The alarm rang out above the sounds of traffic.

These are very common combinations you'll see and hear constantly.

Above all
Means most importantly or more than anything else.

  • Above all, stay calm.
  • She wanted, above all, to be respected.

Above and beyond
Means more than what is expected or required. Used to praise effort.

  • He went above and beyond to help the team.
  • Her work was above and beyond what was asked.

Above suspicion
Means too honest or trustworthy to be suspected of wrongdoing.

  • Her reputation was spotless — she was above suspicion.

Above average
Simply means better than or greater than the average.

  • Her performance was above average.
  • He has above-average intelligence.

Every single use of "above" traces back to one idea: something is at a higher level than something else. Whether that's:

  • a physical object sitting higher in space,
  • a temperature exceeding a number on a scale,
  • a person holding a greater rank,
  • a character too dignified to stoop to something,
  • a value being prioritized over others,
  • or a sound cutting through the noise —

in every case, one thing is elevated relative to another. That is the soul of this word.
